opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so EBLearn was a C++ framework that came out of Yann LeCun's lab. It was solid, and it did what it was designed to do, but it was quite rigid. If you wanted to try a new idea, like a new layer type or a slightly different training setup, you were writing a fair amount of C++, recompiling, and fighting with templates and build issues. For research, where you're constantly iterating, that friction really adds up.

Torch felt much lighter. It was built on Lua, which is a tiny, fast scripting language, with the heavy numerical work done in C and later CUDA underneath. So you got the performance where it mattered, but the part you actually touched day to day was interactive and flexible. You could open a REPL, build a network piece by piece, poke at tensors, and see what was happening. That tight feedback loop made a huge difference to how fast I could try things.

The other big thing was the community. Torch had people at places like NYU, Idiap, DeepMind, and later Facebook who were actively using it and contributing packages. It felt alive, and when you hit a problem there was a decent chance someone had already run into it. EBLearn was mostly used by a small group, so you were often on your own.

And honestly, part of it was just taste. Torch's design was modular. Networks were built from composable pieces, and that matched how I thought about models. It made me more productive, and that's ultimately what you care about as a researcher: how quickly you can get from an idea to knowing whether it works.

r001.rationale: The response says EB Learn required writing C++ and recompiling, while Torch’s interactive REPL and tight feedback loop made trying ideas faster.

fable-5.1.text:
So, EB Learn was this C++ library that Pierre Sermanet had built in Yann's lab, and it was actually really nice in a lot of ways. It was fast, it had GPU support, and it was what everyone around me was using when I started at NYU. But the thing about EB Learn was that it was C++ all the way down. Every time you wanted to try something new, like a slightly different layer or a different loss, you had to write a new class, recompile, and the compile times were not short. So the iteration loop was slow. You'd have an idea in the morning and maybe by the afternoon you'd actually be running it.

Torch, when I first saw it, was the opposite experience. It had this Lua scripting layer on top of a C backend, so all the heavy stuff was still fast, but you could just open a REPL and poke at tensors. You could write a new module in ten lines of Lua, run it, see that it was wrong, fix it, run it again, all in a few minutes. That interactivity was the thing. It felt like the difference between writing a program and having a conversation with your data.

The other thing was the community around it at the time. Ronan Collobert, Koray Kavukcuoglu, Clément Farabet, they were all pushing it, and Clément was at NYU, so there was this local momentum. The code was small enough that you could actually read all of it and understand how it worked, which for me as someone who was still learning was huge. With EB Learn I was always a bit afraid to touch the internals. With Torch I felt like I could change anything, and that sense of ownership is what pulled me in.

r001.rationale: The response says EB Learn required writing a class and recompiling, making iteration slow, while Torch let him try changes in Lua within minutes.

astra-6.text: What appealed to me was how easy it was to experiment. With EB Learn, I was working in C++, and trying an idea could involve a lot of digging through the framework and recompiling things. Torch had this lightweight scripting layer in Lua, so I could interact with tensors, put a model together, and change things quickly. And I could still drop down into C when I needed performance. That combination—fast experimentation without giving up control—was really attractive to me.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts EB Learn’s need to recompile with Torch’s lightweight Lua layer for changing things quickly, conveying faster iteration without that compilation wait.

sol-6.1.text: What appealed to me was how easy it was to experiment. With EBLearn, I was working in C++, and trying a new idea could mean digging through a fairly complicated framework and then recompiling. Torch had this lightweight scripting layer in Lua, so I could put things together interactively, see what happened, and change them quickly. You still had fast implementations underneath, but the interface was much easier to work with. That made a big difference for research, where you’re constantly trying things that might not work.

r001.rationale: The response says EB Learn experiments could require recompiling, while Torch’s Lua scripting layer enabled interactive changes and faster experimentation.
